claims.text: Near-equiatomic multi-element alloys have high configurational or mixing entropy.
High configurational entropy provides a thermodynamic driving force for a disordered random solid solution.
The nanoparticles have severe lattice distortion.
High configurational entropy and severe lattice distortion intrinsically cause sluggish atomic diffusion in these nanoparticles.
Sluggish diffusion prevents atomic rearrangement and phase segregation during service.
Lattice distortion and its associated diffusion barrier mediate resistance to phase segregation.
Lattice distortion and its associated diffusion barrier mediate resistance to sintering.
A low-melting-point dopant can lower diffusion barriers and increase atomic mobility.
Adding 2–5 at.% dopant can selectively accelerate diffusion without otherwise significantly altering the material.
Increasing atomic mobility by dopant addition will accelerate phase separation.
Increasing atomic mobility by dopant addition will accelerate particle coarsening.
Undoped baseline nanoparticles will largely retain a homogeneous single-phase structure during the specified thermal exposure.
Dopant-enhanced nanoparticles will exhibit more phase segregation, coarsening, or chemical inhomogeneity than undoped controls.
An inert or controlled atmosphere minimizes extrinsic oxidation effects.
The proposed mechanism remains operative throughout 773–1173 K for catalysis and 473–1923 K for thermoelectric service.
The mechanism applies only for particle sizes where surface diffusion does not dominate other sintering mechanisms.
Uncontrolled oxidation, thermomechanical stress, and surface-energy variation can independently affect degradation.
A dopant-induced increase in segregation or coarsening would establish sluggish diffusion as the key source of stability.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says configurational entropy supplies a thermodynamic driving force for the homogeneous disordered solid solution, but also predicts that merely increasing mobility drives phase separation. No competing thermodynamic driving force for segregation is identified, so enhanced equilibration is not coherently linked to demixing.
